items.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the cited scattering measures and vocabulary.

**False statement.** *Let a conservative central scattering model with a
finite-range interaction, positive energy and nonzero angular momentum have
a unique scattering angle for every impact parameter. Then the scattering
angle is a strictly decreasing function of the impact parameter.*

The smooth finite-range witness below refutes this claim within the exact
central-scattering class of [[def-cm15-asymptotic-data]]: the zero potential
has deflection $0$ at every positive impact parameter. More generally,
beyond the range of any finite-range potential the scattering trajectories
are free, so a globally defined deflection map has a constant tail. The
separate adopted refracting-shell comparison retains its increasing branch;
that contact rule is outside the smooth $C^2$ class and is not used as the
witness for the stated claim. [[pthm-cm15-central-scattering]] clause 5 makes
no global monotonicity assertion, and [[def-cm15-cross-section]] uses
specified deflection branches instead of inverting a global decreasing map.
items.strategy: Refute global strict decrease with the exact smooth zero-potential free trajectories; separately compute the adopted refracting-shell branch by chord geometry and prove its derivative is positive using a local inverse-sine difference-quotient argument.
items.physical_scope: Assuming countable choice for the scattering measures and vocabulary, the smooth finite-range model has zero deflection for every impact parameter beyond its range, so any globally defined deflection map is constant on this tail and cannot be strictly decreasing. The zero potential is a genuine smooth witness with unique deflection for every positive impact parameter. As a separate example-specific contact model, the adopted attractive refracting shell of index 3/2 has a strictly increasing branch on $0<b<a$ and a jump to zero at grazing incidence $b=a$; the endpoint extension at $b=0$ is not a branch value, and the contact model is outside the smooth central-scattering class and the restricted restitution postulate. All computations concern declared model data and report no observations.

references.title: Konstantin Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Classical Mechanics (title page last edited September 1, 2026), §3.5, the discussion after Eq. (3.69): the assertion that the scattering angle decreases as the particle energy or the impact parameter is increased, the unqualified form of which is refuted here

Richard Fitzpatrick, Newtonian Dynamics (University of Texas at Austin), §6.4, Eqs. (352)-(357): the impenetrable-sphere example, where the deflection is monotone for the reflection contact rule; the contrast with the refracting rule below shows that monotonicity is a property of the interaction rule, not of central scattering as such

items.title: A declared-data impact check: $m_1=2\,\mathrm{kg}$, $m_2=6\,\mathrm{kg}$, $v_1^-=3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $v_2^-=-1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, with elastic, semi-elastic and sticking outcomes
items.statement:
**Declared model data.** Adopt a collinear impact of two labels of the
contact model of [[post-cm15-impulse]] clauses (i)-(ii) along the contact
direction $n$, with masses and incoming velocities
$$m_1=2\ \mathrm{kg},\qquad m_2=6\ \mathrm{kg},\qquad v_1^-=3\,n\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\qquad v_2^-=-1\,n\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} .$$
Thus $M=8\ \mathrm{kg}$, $\mu=\frac{2\cdot6}{8}=\frac32\ \mathrm{kg}$,
$V=\frac{2\cdot3+6\cdot(-1)}{8}=0$, and the relative velocity is
$d^-:=v_2^--v_1^-=-4\,n\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

**Assertions to check.** For $e=1$ (elastic): $v_1^+=-3n$,
$v_2^+=+1n$, $\Delta K=0$. For $e=\frac12$: $v_1^+=-\frac32n$,
$v_2^+=+\frac12n$, impulse $J=-9n\ \mathrm{N\,s}$,
$\Delta K=-9\ \mathrm{J}$. For $e=0$ (sticking): $v_1^+=v_2^+=0$,
$\Delta K=-12\ \mathrm{J}$. In every case the total momentum $P=0$ is
continuous across the impact, as [[pthm-cm15-impact-balance]] clause 1
requires, and the energy changes are those of its clause 4.
items.strategy: A declared-data impact check: elastic, semi-elastic and sticking outcomes for one data set, verifying momentum continuity, the impulse, the velocities and the energy changes.
items.physical_scope: A declared-data check of the adopted collinear impact model: masses $2$ and $6\,\mathrm{kg}$ with one-dimensional velocities $3$ and $-1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ along the contact direction, for coefficients of restitution $e=1,\frac12,0$; the example verifies total momentum continuity, the impulse $J=-9\,\mathrm{N\,s}$ at $e=\frac12$, the post-impact velocities, and the kinetic-energy changes $0,-9,-12\,\mathrm{J}$, all in SI units. Every number is declared model data substituted into the model formulas; the example reports no measurement and no empirical comparison.

references.title: Jacob Moore and Contributors, Mechanics Map (Pennsylvania State University, 2nd ed.), Engineering LibreTexts, §§11.3-11.5: the impulse-momentum principle, momentum conservation and the coefficient-of-restitution treatment of one-dimensional particle collisions

Richard Fitzpatrick, Newtonian Dynamics (University of Texas at Austin), 'Non-Isolated Systems', Eqs. (38)-(44): the momentum and external-force accounting that the impulse model extends to an isolated contact

items.title: A coefficient of restitution above $1$ manufactures kinetic energy: $e=2$ on $m_1=m_2=1\,\mathrm{kg}$ with velocities $\pm1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ raises the kinetic energy by $3\,\mathrm{J}$ while the configuration is unchanged
items.statement:
**False statement.** If the collinear reciprocal-impulse equations of
[[post-cm15-impulse]] clause (i) are retained but its clause (ii) is
**hypothetically extended** to allow every real restitution coefficient $e$,
then momentum conservation and $v_2^+-v_1^+=-e(v_2^--v_1^-)$ guarantee
conservation of total mechanical energy across the impact in a static
central-potential model.

The adopted postulate restricts $e$ to $[0,1]$, as do the restitution and
energy clauses of [[pthm-cm15-impact-balance]] and
[[thm-cm-impulse-restitution-and-energy-loss]]. Those clauses are not
applied at $e=2$ here. The extension is a separate hypothetical law, and the
post-impact velocities and energy difference below are derived locally from
its equations. Only the elastic case $e=1$ guarantees kinetic-energy
conservation for nonzero relative velocity within the adopted range.
items.strategy: A refutation by witness: with e=2 the contact law raises the kinetic energy by 3 J while the configuration is unchanged, so e>1 is incompatible with the conservative energy account.
items.physical_scope: A hypothetical extension of the adopted impact model, replacing only its restitution range by arbitrary real e; a refutation of the claim that every real coefficient of restitution is admissible in the adopted isolated-impact model: with the collinear restitution law and $e=2$ on declared data, the kinetic energy rises by $3\,\mathrm{J}$ across an impact while the configuration is instantaneously unchanged, so the total mechanical energy of a conservative two-label model is not conserved; values $e>1$ therefore signal an omitted internal energy reservoir and are excluded from the conservative contact model of this page, which restricts $e$ to $[0,1]$. The witness uses declared model data and asserts no measurement.

references.title: Jacob Moore and Contributors, Mechanics Map (Pennsylvania State University, 2nd ed.), Engineering LibreTexts, §11.4: the coefficient of restitution between 0 and 1, with the remark that values above 1 would describe a superelastic collision in which additional stored energy is released

Richard Fitzpatrick, Newtonian Dynamics (University of Texas at Austin), §6.5, Eqs. (368)-(396): the elastic two-body collision with kinetic energy preserved, the conservative case against which the superelastic witness is contrasted

items.title: Reciprocal impulses do not determine a collinear impact: the same incoming data admit the sticking outcome $v^+=0$ and the elastic outcome $(v_1^+,v_2^+)=(-3,1)\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ with different impulses and energies
items.statement:
**False statement.** *In the collinear isolated-impact model of
[[post-cm15-impulse]] clause (i), the reciprocal impulse equations
$m_1(v_1^+-v_1^-)=J$ and $m_2(v_2^+-v_2^-)=-J$, with the impulse $J$
determined by momentum balance of the two labels, fix the post-impact
velocities for given incoming data; no additional contact law is needed.*

[[post-cm15-impulse]] clause (ii) adopts the restitution law as an
*independent* contact assumption, and [[pthm-cm15-impact-balance]] clause 5
records that the impulse equations leave the scalar impulse magnitude free.
The witness exhibits two admissible outcomes for one data set.
items.strategy: A refutation by witness: two admissible outcomes with different impulses satisfy the same reciprocal impulse equations, so an independent contact law is required.
items.physical_scope: A refutation of the claim that the reciprocal impulse equations alone determine a collinear impact: with masses $2$ and $6\,\mathrm{kg}$ and incoming velocities $3$ and $-1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, both the sticking outcome and the elastic outcome satisfy the equal-and-opposite momentum jumps with impulses $-6\,\mathrm{N\,s}$ and $-12\,\mathrm{N\,s}$ respectively and total momentum $0$, while velocities and kinetic-energy changes differ. Hence the contact law fixing the impulse (or the coefficient of restitution) is an independent model datum. The witness uses declared model data and asserts no measurement, no determination of any real coefficient and no observation.

references.title: Jacob Moore and Contributors, Mechanics Map (Pennsylvania State University, 2nd ed.), Engineering LibreTexts, §11.5 'Particle Collisions in One Dimension': conservation of momentum as the first equation and an independent second relation (energy or restitution) as the second, the structure the witness exploits

J. Peraire and S. Widnall, 16.07 Dynamics (MIT OpenCourseWare, Fall 2008/2009), Lecture L14: the discrete mass-loss examples in which the final velocity depends on the adopted ejection rule, the finite version of the underdetermination recorded here

items.title: A declared rocket check: initial mass $3\,\mathrm{kg}$, loss rate $1\,\mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$ and relative exhaust speed $2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ give $v=u_e\ln(m_0/m)n$ and show that $(mv)'=F$ fails
items.statement:
**Declared model data.** Adopt the open-body material accounting of
[[post-cm15-impulse]] clause (iii) with, on the open interval
$I=(-\frac12\ \mathrm s,\frac52\ \mathrm s)$ containing the initial time $0$,
set $m_0:=3\ \mathrm{kg}$, $r_0:=1\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$, and
$$m(t):=m_0-r_0t,\qquad F\equiv0,\qquad r_{\mathrm{in}}\equiv0,\qquad r_{\mathrm{out}}\equiv r_0,\qquad w_{\mathrm{out}}(t):=v(t)-u_e\,n,$$
with a fixed unit vector $n$, $u_e:=2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and initial
velocity $v(0)=0$. The ejecta therefore leave with the body's velocity
reduced by the constant exhaust speed $u_e$ along $n$. Set
$q:=t/(1\ \mathrm s)$, the dimensionless numerical time, so
$m(t)=(3-q)\ \mathrm{kg}$. Primes denote differentiation with respect to
physical frame time $t$, read in seconds.

**Assertions to check.** The balance identities hold with
$$v(t)=u_e\ln\frac{m_0}{m(t)}\,n=2\ln\frac{3}{3-q}\ n\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\qquad(t\in I),$$
the thrust is $r_{\mathrm{out}}u_e=2\ \mathrm{N}$ along $n$, and the naive
closed-system law $(mv)'=F$ fails: it would force $v\equiv0$ on $I$.
items.strategy: A declared-data check of the open-body law: linear mass loss with constant relative exhaust speed gives the Tsiolkovsky velocity and shows that the closed-system law fails.
items.physical_scope: A declared-data check of the open-body material accounting: a body of initial mass $m_0=3\,\mathrm{kg}$ losing mass at $r_0=1\,\mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$ has $m(t)=m_0-r_0t$. With no external force and ejecta of relative speed $u_e=2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ opposite a fixed unit direction $n$, its velocity from rest is $v(t)=u_e\ln(m_0/m(t))n$. It satisfies the material balance identities and violates the naive closed-system law $(mv)'=F$; the example verifies the identities, the thrust $2\,\mathrm{N}$ and the failure of the naive law on declared model data. It reports no measurement, no engine data and no empirical comparison.

references.title: J. Peraire and S. Widnall, 16.07 Dynamics (MIT OpenCourseWare, Fall 2008/2009), Lecture L14 'Variable Mass Systems: The Rocket Equation', Eqs. (11)-(15): $m\,\mathrm d\mathbf v/\mathrm dt=\mathbf F+(\mathrm dm/\mathrm dt)\mathbf v_0$ with $\mathbf v_0$ the transferred matter's velocity relative to the body, and the Tsiolkovsky integral
David Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge), §1.2, printed p. 2: the caution that the closed-system form of the momentum balance does not describe an open variable-mass body

items.title: A declared smooth open flow: the uniform scaling $\rho=\rho_0e^{-3\alpha t}$, $u=\alpha x$ satisfies the control-volume identities on fixed and material regions, and elbow port data illustrate the inlet/outlet decomposition
items.statement:
**(i) Declared uniform scaling.** Fix constants $\rho_0>0$,
$\alpha\ne0$ and $p_0$, with $[\rho_0]=\mu\ell^{-3}$,
$[\alpha]=\tau^{-1}$ and $[p_0]=\mu\ell^{-1}\tau^{-2}$. On an open
interval $I\ni0$ use uniform scaling, meaning expansion for $\alpha>0$
and contraction for $\alpha<0$, and set
$$\rho(t)=\rho_0e^{-3\alpha t},\qquad u(t,x)=\alpha x,\qquad \sigma(t,x)=-p(t,x)\,\mathrm{Id},\qquad p(t,x)=p_0-\frac{\rho(t)\alpha^2}{2}\lvert x\rvert^2,\qquad b\equiv0,$$
and fix radii $R_0>0$ and $R>0$ with units $\ell$. Let the material region
be a ball $B_{R_B}$ with radius $R_B>\max(R,R_0)$.
Define the material motion $\chi(t,X)=e^{\alpha t}X$ on a neighbourhood of
$\overline{B_{R_B}}$. More precisely, choose an open ball $O=B_{R_O}$ with
$R_O>R_B$ and define $\chi:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ by this formula.
Its restriction to $B_{R_0}$ has current radius
$R(t)=R_0e^{\alpha t}$. Define the fixed-ball control motion by
$\psi_R(t,X)=X$ for $X\in O$, with control region $B_R$, and the
material-ball control motion by $\psi_{\mathrm{mat}}(t,X)=e^{\alpha t}X$
for $X\in O$, with control region $B_{R_0}$. Each map is a $C^2$ motion on
the open reference domain $O$ and has positive spatial Jacobian. Take the
fields on a common open neighbourhood of
the closed sweep of $\chi$ and the closed sweeps of these controls. The fields
satisfy the adopted balances of
[[pthm-cm15-control-volume-balance]] (the density is spatially uniform, the
velocity is $\alpha x$, and the pressure is quadratic).

**(ii) Declared elbow control-volume data.** Take a material region $B$ with
motion $\chi$ and associated spatial velocity field $u$ as in
[[def-cm-continuum-motion]], and a material subregion $B'\subseteq B$ with
$C^1$ boundary. On an open reference neighbourhood
$O\supset\overline{B'}$, define the fixed control motion
$\psi:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ by $\psi(t,X)=X$; its control region is
$C_t=C:=B'$ and its boundary velocity is $w=0$. Adopt the material balances
of [[pthm-cm15-control-volume-balance]] for this model and the local mass and
momentum equations on an open field neighbourhood of the closed control
region, as allowed by that theorem's local-equation alternative.

Assume $\rho=1000\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$ is constant and the fields are
time-independent on that neighbourhood. The bounded $C^1$ boundary of $C$
is partitioned into finitely many $C^1$ boundary pieces, up to
surface-measure-zero edges; designate an inlet patch $\Sigma_{\mathrm{in}}$,
an outlet patch $\Sigma_{\mathrm{out}}$, and let the remaining pieces form
an impermeable remainder $\Sigma_0$. The outward unit normals on the ports are $-\hat x$ and $+\hat y$.
On the ports take $u=q_{\mathrm{in}}\hat x$ and
$u=q_{\mathrm{out}}\hat y$, respectively, where each $q$ is a
nonnegative, nonzero $C^1$ profile supported compactly inside its port,
with units $\ell\tau^{-1}$; take $u\cdot\nu=0$ on the remainder.
These traces vanish near the port edges and are compatible with a
$C^1$ field and continuous boundary normal. For either port define
$$Q:=\int_{\Sigma}q\,\mathrm dS>0,\qquad v_{\mathrm{eff}}:=\frac{\int_{\Sigma}q^2\,\mathrm dS}{Q},\qquad A_{\mathrm{eff}}:=\frac{Q^2}{\int_{\Sigma}q^2\,\mathrm dS},$$
so $Q=A_{\mathrm{eff}}v_{\mathrm{eff}}$, the mass rate is $\rho Q$,
and the flux-averaged velocity is $v_{\mathrm{eff}}$ in the port direction.
Declare $A_{\mathrm{eff,in}}=10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2}$,
$A_{\mathrm{eff,out}}=5\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m^2}$ and
$v_{\mathrm{eff,in}}=4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the outlet effective
speed is unknown. The effective areas are defined by these integrals,
not the geometric patch areas. Assume the time-independent velocity
field is $C^1$ on the common neighbourhood. Set the body-force field to $b=0$ and assume
the stress field is $C^1$ on the same neighbourhood. These are conditional
model premises for a balance calculation; no existence claim for a
boundary-value solution or decomposition of the boundary stress is made.
The calculation determines only the net external resultant required by the
steady balance.
items.strategy: Two declared checks: the exact uniform-expansion field satisfies the control-volume identities on fixed and material balls, and the ideal elbow illustrates the inlet/outlet decomposition with the dynamic force.
items.physical_scope: Two declared checks of the finite-regularity open-flow bookkeeping: (i) the exact uniform-scaling model $\rho(t)=\rho_0e^{-3\alpha t}$, $u(t,x)=\alpha x$, $p=p_0-\rho\alpha^2\lvert x\rvert^2/2$, with the control maps specified and the units of $\alpha,\rho_0,p_0$ declared; (ii) a conditional steady-elbow calculation with declared inlet/outlet data, where the balance gives mass flow $0.4\,\mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}$ and requires a net external resultant on the fluid of magnitude about $3.578\,\mathrm N$. No pressure-free momentum-flux force decomposition is inferred, since no boundary-stress data are given. Both are computations on declared model data; the example reports no measurement and does not solve a boundary-value problem.

W. Barsukow, Introduction to Conservation Laws: Theory and Numerics (lecture notes, TUM, Winter term 2021/22), §§1.1-1.3: the fixed-volume and Lagrangian descriptions of the same balance, used for the fixed-ball and material-ball checks

Jacob Moore and Contributors, Mechanics Map (Pennsylvania State University, 2nd ed.), Engineering LibreTexts, §11.7 'Steady-Flow Devices': the mass-flow relation $\dot m=\rho vA$ and the steady-flow momentum relation used in the elbow illustration
